In mathematics, a '''sparse polynomial''' (also '''lacunary polynomial'''{{r|redei}} or '''fewnomial'''{{r|few}}) is a [[polynomial]] that has far fewer terms than its [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] and number of [[variable (mathematics)|variables]] would suggest. For example, <math>x^{10} + 3x^3 + 1</math> is a sparse polynomial, as it is a [[trinomial]] with a [[Degree of a polynomial|degree]] of <math>10</math>.

The motivation for studying sparse polynomials is to concentrate on the structure of a polynomial's monomials instead of its degree, as one can see, for instance, by comparing [[Bernstein–Kushnirenko theorem]] with [[Bézout's theorem]]. Research on sparse polynomials has also included work on [[algorithm]]s whose running time grows as a function of the number of terms rather than on the degree,{{r|roche}} for problems including [[polynomial multiplication]]{{r|nakos}}{{r|ggpdc20}}, [[Polynomial division|division]],{{r|ggpdc21}} [[root-finding algorithms]],{{r|pan}} and [[polynomial greatest common divisor]]s.{{r|zippel}} Sparse polynomials have also been used in pure mathematics, especially in the study of [[Galois group]]s, because it has been easier to determine the Galois groups of certain families of sparse polynomials than it is for other polynomials.{{r|galois}} 

The [[algebraic variety|algebraic varieties]] determined by sparse polynomials have a simple structure, which is also reflected in the structure of the solutions of certain related [[differential equation]]s.{{r|few}} Additionally, a sparse [[positivstellensatz]] exists for univariate sparse polynomials. It states that the non-negativity of a polynomial can be certified by [[Polynomial SOS|SOS polynomials]] whose degree only depends on the number of monomials of the polynomial.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Averkov |first1=Gennadiy |last2=Scheiderer |first2=Claus |date=2023-03-07 |title=Convex hulls of monomial curves, and a sparse positivstellensatz |class=math.OC |eprint=2303.03826 }}</ref>

Sparse polynomials often come up in sum or difference of powers equations. The [[sum of two cubes]] states that <math>(x + y)(x^2 - xy + y^2) = x^3 + y^3</math>. Here <math>x^3 + y^3</math> is a sparse polynomial, since out of the <math>16</math> possible terms, only <math>2</math> appear.
Other examples include the identities <math>(x - y) \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} x^k y^{N-1-k} = x^N - y^N</math> and also <math>(x + y) \sum_{k=0}^{2n}(-1)^k x^k y^{2n-k} = x^{2n+1} + y^{2n+1},</math> where the product of two polynomials give a sparse polynomial. The [[Bring_radical#Bring–Jerrard_normal_form|Bring–Jerrard normal form]] of a quintic, <math>x^5 + px + q,</math> is also a sparse polynomial.
